# Jeremiah 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview / Setting

This chapter is widely regarded as Jeremiah's inaugural public sermon. The Pulpit Commentary notes that it introduces a group of discourses (Jeremiah 2–6) and was likely delivered in the thirteenth year of Josiah's reign. It takes the form of a divine lawsuit (a "covenant lawsuit" or *rîb*), in which God brings formal charges against His unfaithful people.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Josiah's reformation in the strict sense did not begin until the eighteenth year of his reign; the state of things was complicated by a dangerous Egyptian alliance. The first section is a general introduction full of serious charges (vv. 1–9); the second rebukes the special sin (vv. 10–19); the third denounces Judah's inveterate idolatry (vv. 20–28); the fourth satirically points the moral of the Egyptian fever (vv. 29–37). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-2.html]

- **JFB:** Probably in the thirteenth year of Josiah. The warning not to rely on Egypt was in accordance with Josiah's policy, who took part with Assyria and Babylon against Egypt (2 Kings 23:29). Jeremiah doubtless supported the reformation begun by Josiah. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** This discourse is of a quite general character; it only sketches the main thoughts extended in the following discourses. "In its finished completeness it gives the impression of a first-uttered outpouring of the heart." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/jeremiah-2.html]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The chapter is structured in the imagery of a lawsuit (cf. vv. 4-8, 9, 12, 29; Isa 1:2, 18; Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

---

## Verses 1–3: "The Good Old Days"

**v. 1 — "Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying"**
This is the standard prophetic formula designating that the message originates from YHWH, not the prophet himself. Gill notes this marks the beginning of Jeremiah's first sermon; the Targum calls it "the word of the prophecy from before the Lord." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/2.htm]

**v. 2 — "Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem... I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God made a heartfelt appeal to Jerusalem, drawing upon the memory of their past relationship. "God recollects those zealous times... and if we have come to an ebb... God has not forgotten them" (citing Spurgeon). The reference is to the Exodus when Israel followed God through the wilderness; though not perfect, they had a love and trust for God sorely lacking in Jeremiah's day. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** The "kindness" is not so much Israel's kindness toward God as the kindness which Israel *experienced* from God in their early history (cf. Ezek 16:8, 22, 60). For Israel from the first showed perversity rather than kindness. The "espousals" refer to the interval between Israel's betrothal to God at the Exodus and the formal marriage covenant at Sinai. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Gill:** The "kindness" can be understood either as God's lovingkindness shown to Israel or Israel's responsive love. He notes that the covenant at Sinai was "in the form of a marriage contract; he became their husband, and they became his spouse and bride." The whole may be applied to God's people at first conversion, when love is ardent and fervent — and God remembers this even when they have forgotten. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/2.htm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The rabbis called this period "the honeymoon" between YHWH (husband) and Israel (wife). He provided every need: food, water, clothing, shade, personal guidance. This strophe is like Rev 2:4 — Israel, like the church at Ephesus, had "left her first love." The Hebrew word for "devotion" is *hesed* (lovingkindness/covenant loyalty). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 3 — "Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of His harvest. All who devoured her found themselves guilty; disaster came upon them."**

- **Enduring Word:** In this season of special relationship, God took special care of Israel. If anyone attempted to devour Israel, disaster would come upon them — a great contrast to the judgment that would eventually come upon an unfaithful Jerusalem. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The "firstfruits" imagery alludes to the offering that symbolized YHWH's ownership of the whole crop (Lev 23:10–11; cf. 1 Cor 15:20; James 1:18). The nations that attacked Israel were rejecting YHWH by rejecting His chosen vessel. The term "ate" was used in Akkadian for an "illegal invasion." [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **JFB:** As the firstfruits of the land were devoted to God (Exod 23:19; Num 18:12–13), so Israel was devoted to Him as the representative nation among all nations. All who ate (injured) Jehovah's firstfruits contracted guilt — e.g., Amalek and the Amorites were extirpated for their guilt toward Israel. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Pulpit Commentary (Ellicott):** The word for "offend" (or "found themselves guilty") is the same Hebrew term used for "trespass" — foreigners were forbidden to eat consecrated things; by breaking this law they invaded the rights of Jehovah (Lev 22:10, 15, 16). [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/2.htm]

---

## Verses 4–8: The Great Ingratitude of Rebellious Israel

**v. 4 — "Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all you families of the house of Israel."**

- **Bible.org (Utley):** "Hear" is the theologically significant verb *Shema* (Qal imperative) — "to hear, so as to do." It has great importance in Deut 4:1; 5:1; 6:3–4. Jeremiah was deeply influenced by Deuteronomy. "House of Jacob" and "families of the house of Israel" are parallel phrases for all the seed of Abraham after the split of the United Monarchy in 922 BC. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **JFB:** The call is to the whole nation — "Hear God's word not only collectively, but individually (Zech 12:12–14)." [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 5 — "What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me, and followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves?"**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God called Israel to account, asking what fault there was in Him that caused their idolatry. "Various attempts have been made to render this in English: 'pursuing empty phantoms and themselves becoming empty' (NEB); 'they went after worthlessness and became worthless' (RSV)" (citing Thompson). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "An idol is not only vain (impotent and empty), but vanity itself. Its worshippers acquire its character, becoming vain as it is (Deut 7:26; Ps 115:8). A people's character never rises above that of its gods, which are its 'better nature'" (citing Bacon). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** This is legal imagery of a court scene (cf. Mic 6:3). YHWH's true nature is expressed in Deut 32:4. "He was not the problem, they were!" Note the personal element: "not just follow my laws but follow 'Me'! Biblical faith is a personal faith, in a personal God." The verb "went far from Me" is in direct contradiction to "follow after Me" in v. 2. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 6 — "They did not ask, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt...'"**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Israel failed even to ask the question. They didn't seek the God who had done so much for them. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "The very words which God uses (Isa 63:9, 11, 13), when, as it were, reminding Himself of His former acts of love to Israel as a ground for interposing in their behalf again. When they would not say, Where is Jehovah, etc., God Himself at last said it for them." The "shadow of death" refers to the darkness of the caverns amid rocky precipices (Deut 8:15; 32:10). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 7 — "I brought you into a fertile land to eat its fruit and bounty, but you came and defiled My land, and made My inheritance detestable."**

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Palestine in this period was very fertile (cf. Num 13:23–24, 27; Deut 8:1–9; 11:10–12). "Defiled" is used of sexual defilement, murder, idolatry, and ceremonial uncleanness. "Notice this is God's land and He will not tolerate those who live inappropriately (cf. Lev 18:24–30). As He removed the Canaanites... He will remove Abraham's seed if they reject Him." [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **JFB:** "Plentiful" is literally "a land of Carmel," i.e., a garden land, in contrast to the "land of deserts" (v. 6). The change from third person ("they," v. 6) to second person ("you... ye") is designed "to bring home the guilt to the living generation." [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 8 — "The priests did not ask, 'Where is the LORD?' The experts in the law no longer knew Me, and the leaders rebelled against Me. The prophets prophesied by Baal and followed useless idols."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The religious leaders did not serve God or the people well. "Those who handle the law" (or "draw out the law," as Clarke renders it) refers to priests and Levites whose office was to teach, exposit, interpret, and apply the law. Civic and religious leaders did more harm than good. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** A terrible condemnation of leadership: priests (temple administration), those handling the law (Levites who taught — later "scribes"), rulers (lit. "shepherds" — civil leadership), and prophets. Their sins: questioning YHWH's presence, lacking personal relationship with Him ("did not know Me"), transgressing His law, prophesying by Baal, and walking after things that do not profit. There may be a sound play in Hebrew between "profitless" (*ya'al*) and "Baal" (*ba'al*). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **JFB:** The three leading classes, whose very office under the theocracy was to lead the people to God, disowned Him in the same language as the nation at large. Prophets "should have reclaimed the people from their apostasy, encouraged them in it by pretended oracles from Baal." [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Gill:** "The pastors" are interpreted as kings (so Targum, Jarchi, Kimchi) — shepherds in a civil sense whose business was to guide and govern the people by God's laws, but instead they rebelled against the Lord. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/2.htm]

---

## Verses 9–13: The Astonishing Nature of Israel's Sin

**v. 9 — "Therefore, I will contend with you again... and I will bring a case against your children's children."**

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The verb "contend" (repeated twice, Qal imperfect) refers to a legal lawsuit. This shows that lifestyle priorities are passed on to children with resulting blessing or cursing (Exod 34:7; Deut 5:9). Utley rejoices that Deut 7:9 extends God's love to "thousand generations" of those who love Him. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **JFB:** Three manuscripts and Jerome omit "children's"; but "it is designedly so written, to intimate that the final judgment on the nation would be suspended for many generations" (Horsley). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 10 — "Cross over to the coasts of Cyprus and take a look; send to Kedar and consider carefully; see if there has ever been anything like this."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Cyprus was the western-most point in Judah's geography, whilst Kedar was a desert tribe in the east, so the appeal is from west to east, i.e. anywhere" (citing Cundall). Since Israel liked to imitate surrounding nations in idolatry, God asked them to look even to distant places and ask: Do those nations forsake their gods? [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Kittim originally referred to the Phoenician settlement on Cyprus but came to mean all islands west of Palestine. Kedar was an Arab tribe to the east. The phrase is used metaphorically for "from east to west" — meaning "Ask anyone!" [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **Gill:** The Jewish writers say the Kedarenes worshipped water and the Chittim fire; though water quenches fire, neither would change their gods. Kimchi and Abendana relate it in reverse (Kedarenes, fire; Chittim, water). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/2.htm]

**v. 11 — "Has a nation ever changed its gods, though they are no gods at all? Yet My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The heathen nations were faithful to their gods even though their gods did nothing for them. Yet Israel had the God of all Glory who had blessed them in innumerable ways, and they turned from Him. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "Glory" — i.e., Jehovah, the glory of Israel (Ps 106:20; Rom 1:23). The Shekinah cloud resting on the sanctuary was the symbol of "the glory of the Lord" (1 Kgs 8:11; cf. Rom 9:4). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** "Their glory" — NKJV and NRSV capitalize "Glory," showing it is a characteristic title for God (cf. Rom 1:23). "He was Israel's glory! When they reject Him they have no glory (cf. Hos 4:7)." [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 12 — "Be stunned by this, O heavens; be shocked and utterly appalled," declares the LORD.**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** First this is an astonishment (that men can be so foolish, disloyal, and ungrateful), then something to fear (a righteous God must answer such rebellion), finally a desolation (the result of judgment will leave little behind). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The heavens are often used as witnesses in God's lawsuit (cf. Deut 4:26; 30:19; 32:1). YHWH directs the oldest witness with three Qal imperatives: be appalled, shudder, be very desolate (lit. "dry up"). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 13 — "For My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns — broken cisterns that cannot hold water."**

This is the thematic heart of the chapter and one of Jeremiah's most famous images.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The first evil is to forsake God, which is not only disloyal and ungrateful but also foolish — God is the never-ending supply of good, pure, essential supplies of life. In the ancient Near East, an artesian spring ("fountain of living waters") was something special: a constant supply that came to you. The second evil: having forsaken the fountain, they worked hard (hewn themselves) for a greatly inferior supply, and what they ended up with was broken — "Directly water is stored in cisterns, it ceases to be living; it is stagnant, and the process of deterioration begins... Moreover, man can never hew cisterns which will hold. They are all broken. We must live by streams, or we perish" (citing Morgan). Guzik also quotes F.B. Meyer: "Leaving God... he hath set himself, with infinite labour, to hew out cisterns of gold and silver, cisterns of splendid houses and reputable characters... At the best, however, the water is brackish." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** The Hebrew collocation brings God into prominent contrast: "Me they have forsaken, the Fountain..." Cisterns were tanks for rainwater common in the East where wells are scarce. The tanks cannot give an ever-flowing fresh supply like fountains, and when the stonework is broken, the earth drinks up the collected water. "So, in general, all earthly, compared with heavenly, means of satisfying man's highest wants (Isa 55:1–2; cf. Luke 12:33)." [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** "Fountain of living waters" is a descriptive title for God (cf. 17:13; Ps 36:9; John 4:10–14; 7:38–39; Rev 21:6). "This is the problem of fallen humanity, even covenant humanity. They try to run their own lives (cf. vv. 17, 19). Their failure will open the door for YHWH's mercy and grace in the 'new covenant' of Jer 31:31–34 (cf. Ezek 36:22–38)." [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **Gill:** Grace in Christ is compared to water (cooling, refreshing, cleansing, fructifying) and to living water because it quickens dead sinners, revives drooping saints, and issues in eternal life; it is perpetual and ever-flowing. The "cisterns" include the world and its things, the inventions and ordinances of men, moral duties and evangelical services when depended on, even spiritual frames when lived upon instead of Christ. "It is egregious folly to leave a fountain for a cistern, and especially a broken one: in a fountain the water is living, and always running... not so in a cistern, and in a broken cistern there is none at all." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/2.htm]

---

## Verses 14–19: God's People Look to Egypt and Assyria and Forsake the LORD

**v. 14 — "Is Israel a slave? Was he born into slavery? Why then has he become prey?"**

- **JFB:** "Israel is Jehovah's son, even His first-born" (Exod 4:22). "How comes it to pass that the nation which once was under God's special protection (v. 3) is now left at the mercy of the foe as a worthless slave?" The prophet sees this event as if present, though still future to Judah. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bridgeway:** "Israel and Judah boasted that they were God's children, but now they are becoming slaves of other nations." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-2.html]

**v. 15 — "The young lions have roared at him; they have growled with a loud voice. They have laid waste his land; his cities lie in ruins, without inhabitant."**

- **JFB:** "Lions" — the Babylonian princes (Jer 4:7; cf. Amos 3:4). The disaster from the Babylonians in the fourth year of Jehoiakim's reign, and again three years later when he revolted from Nebuchadnezzar relying on Egypt, is here referred to. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Young lions are a metaphor of power and strength — top predators symbolizing invading enemies. "Without her God, she was vulnerable and weak! The false gods who could not see or hear, could not help!" The MT has "burned" (*nitsethah*), but the Masoretic scholars suggested a reading meaning "are in ruins." Both options fit synonymous parallelism. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 16 — "The men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Noph (Memphis) was the ancient capital of lower Egypt, near modern Cairo. Tahpanhes was an Egyptian frontier city. God warned Judah not to trust in Egypt, which would (or had by that time) "broken the crown of your head" by defeating and killing good King Josiah in battle (2 Kgs 23:29). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** Memphis (from Man-nofri, "the abode of good men") and Tahpanhes (Daphne, on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, named from the goddess Tphnet) stand for the whole of Egypt. The reference includes Pharaoh-necho's invasion, when he deposed Jehoahaz and levied heavy tribute (2 Kgs 23:33–35). Josiah's death in battle is probably included. The "shaving" (or "breaking") signifies the greatest ignominy, as baldness was regarded in the East (Jer 48:37; 2 Kgs 2:23). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 17 — "Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God when He led you in the way?"**

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Israel is reaping what she sowed (cf. 17:10; 32:19). The rhetorical question answers v. 14. The Septuagint has a different line: "'Has not your abandoning of Me brought about these things for you?' says the Lord God." [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **JFB:** "Has not thy forsaking the Lord... procured this (calamity) to thee?" The article in "the way" expresses the right way — the moral training they enjoyed in the Mosaic covenant. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 18 — "Now what will you gain on your way to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? What will you gain on your way to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates?"**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God cautioned Jerusalem from looking to either Egypt ("waters of Sihor" = the Nile) or Assyria ("waters of the River" = the Euphrates) for help. "Sihor, 'blackness', is a sarcastic reference to the river Nile, one of the most highly venerated of Egyptian gods" (citing Harrison). "No matter how appealing the prospect of alliance with Egypt might be, Judah will suffer for it if she becomes entangled" (Harrison). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "Sihor" = the black river (Greek *Melas*), i.e., the Nile, so called from the black deposit left after inundation. "The river" = Euphrates, called by pre-eminence "the river," figurative for Assyrian/Babylonian power. In 625 BC (the seventeenth year of Josiah), Assyria fell before Babylon; thus Assyria here stands for Babylon its successor. Josiah's league with Babylon caused him to march against Pharaoh-necho. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** "To drink the water" is a metaphor for voluntary service of another — in a sense, "self-imposed exile." These alliances included ceremonies with national idols. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 19 — "Your own evil will discipline you; your own apostasies will reprimand you. Consider and realize how evil and bitter it is for you to forsake the LORD your God and to have no fear of Me," declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** If Jerusalem continued on their destructive course, there would be more than enough correction and rebuke found in the consequences of their actions. Jerusalem feared attack from Babylon and contemplated alliances with Egypt and Assyria, yet "the real problem was they did not fear the LORD, and the Lord GOD of hosts — that is, of heavenly armies. God was more than able to protect them if they repented and trusted in Him." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Like vv. 13 and 17, this emphasizes the terrible results of Israel's choices (cf. 4:18). YHWH responds with two Qal imperatives ("know" and "see") — they will realize the consequences of leaving YHWH and embracing idolatry. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **Precept Austin devotionals:** This verse summarizes the state of things — God reminds them "how evil and bitter it is" to forsake the Lord. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_devotionals-1]

---

## Verses 20–25: The Unrestrained Pursuit of False Gods

**v. 20 — "For long ago you broke your yoke and tore off your chains, saying, 'I will not serve!' Indeed, on every high hill and under every green tree you lay down as a prostitute."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Israel's idolatry is pictured as prostitution. Many pagan and Canaanite idols were essentially sex cults honored with ritual prostitution. "The many references to abnormal sexual gratification underline one of the most prominent features of the Canaanite religion, where male and female cult-prostitutes were connected with the sanctuaries" (citing Cundall). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** The Hebrew should probably be read as second person feminine: "Thou hast broken thy yoke..." (so LXX). "The yoke and bands which I laid on thee, My laws (Jer 5:5)." The "hill... green tree" were the scenes of idolatries (Deut 12:2; Isa 57:5, 7). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Lines 1–2 speak of the Exodus, when God formed Israel into a nation. Israel traded the slavery of Egypt for the slavery of Mesopotamia. Lines 4–6 refer to the pervasiveness of the fertility cult of Baal and Asherah (cf. 3:2, 6; Deut 16:21; Hos 4:11–14). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 21 — "I had planted you like a choice vine from the very best seed. How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?"**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The noble (AV) or choice (RSV) vine is literally, 'Sorek vine', a high-quality red grape grown in the Wadi al-Sarar" (Harrison). "God has planted his people a thoroughly reliable stock hoping to gather a rich harvest of choice grapes. But she became a strange wild vine, a foul-smelling thing" (Thompson). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** *Sorek* (BDB 977 I) means "red grape," one of the best varieties (cf. Isa 5:1–7). But Israel "turned yourself" into "the degenerate shoots of a foreign vine." [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 22 — "Although you wash with lye and use an abundance of soap, the stain of your guilt is still before Me," declares the Lord GOD.**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Sin leaveth behind it a deep stain, so ingrained that it will hardly ever be gotten out, not at all by blanching, extenuating, excusing, etc., or by any legal purifications, hypocritical lotions" (Trapp). "So ingrained is Judah's foul iniquity that no amount of washing with detergents can remove it. The supreme merit of Christ's work on Calvary is that it removes the dark stain of iniquity (1 John 1:7)" (Harrison). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "Nitre" is not modern saltpeter but the natron of Egypt, a mineral alkali used for washing (cf. Job 9:30; Prov 25:20). "Soap" is potash (carbonate), obtained impure from burning plants, especially the kali of Egypt and Arabia. Mixed with oil, it was used for washing. "Marked" = deeply ingrained, indelibly marked. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 23 — "How can you say, 'I am not defiled; I have not run after the Baals'? Look at your behavior in the valley; acknowledge what you have done. You are a swift young she-camel galloping here and there."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The valley" refers to the Valley of Hinnom, the deep gorge west and south of Jerusalem — a place of hideous idolatry. "Here all sorts of heathen rites were practiced, including the worship of Baal and the worship of Molech (cf. 7:31–32; 2 Kgs 23:10)" (Thompson). "How could they claim innocence when they were carrying on their vile worship of Baal in the Valley of Hinnom with their child sacrifices?" (Feinberg). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Self-deception is the worst possible blindness (cf. Prov 16:2; 30:12; Luke 16:15; 18:9–14). The valley is probably Ben Hinnom where Molech was worshipped by child sacrifice (cf. Lev 18:21). "Young female camels are altogether unreliable, ungainly, and easily disturbed, so that they dash about in an apparently disorganized fashion" (Thompson). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 24 — "...a wild donkey at home in the wilderness, sniffing the wind in the heat of her desire. Who can restrain her passion? All who seek her need not weary themselves; in mating season they will find her."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The image is of a camel or wild donkey in heat, with no control over her desire, allowing any and all to mount her. "The female ass in heat is almost violent. She sniffs the path in front of her trying to pick up the scent of a male (from his urine). Then she races down the road in search of the male" (Thompson). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "At her pleasure" — rather, "in her ardor," namely, in pursuit of a male, sniffing the wind to ascertain where one is to be found (Maurer). "Her month" — in the season of the year when her sexual impulse is strongest, she puts herself in the way of the males, so they have no difficulty finding her. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 25 — "You should have kept your feet from going bare and your throat from being thirsty. But you said, 'It is hopeless! For I love foreign gods, and I must go after them.'"**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The bare foot and constant thirst were marks of the exile and slave — the fate of the northern kingdom and potentially Judah. Yet they answered God's heartfelt appeal with resignation to their idolatry: "There is no hope... I have loved aliens and after them I will go." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "Withhold, etc." — that is, abstain from incontinence; figuratively for idolatry (Houbigant). Do not run so violently in pursuing lovers as to wear out your shoes. "No hope" (Jer 18:12; Isa 57:10) — "It is hopeless," i.e., I am desperately resolved to go on in my own course. "Strangers" — laying aside the metaphor, "strange gods" (Jer 3:13; Deut 32:16). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

## Verses 26–28: The Shame of Israel

**v. 26 — "As the thief is ashamed when he is caught, so the house of Israel is disgraced. They, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets..."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The thief is only ashamed when found out — he regrets getting caught and penalized, not the crime itself. In the same way, Israel under exile was really only sorry they had been caught and suffered for their sin. All ranks — kings, princes, priests, prophets — are included. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** These are the same leaders mentioned in v. 8. Fear of shame was a powerful motivation for Eastern people (cf. 15:9; 31:19; 48:13, 39; Isa 1:29). [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**v. 27 — "...say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their backs to Me and not their faces, yet in the time of trouble they beg, 'Rise up and save us!'"**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The tree was a wooden idol representing Asherah (the leading female Canaanite deity); the stone represented Baal (the leading male deity). "At each Canaanite shrine there was an asherah, probably a wooden pillar which was a formal substitute for a sacred tree, representing the female sexual element, and a mazzebah, or stone pillar, indicating the male element" (Cundall). "There is strong satire here, for it is the female symbol [tree] that is called Father and the male symbol [stone] that is called 'You who gave me birth.' Israel was confused about what she was worshipping" (Thompson). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** This is a play on the symbols of Canaanite fertility gods: Baal symbolized by an uplifted stone (phallus), Asherah by a carved stake or live tree (tree of life). In v. 28, two imperatives ("arise," "save us") mock what idol worshippers said to their non-existent idols. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 28 — "But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can; for your gods are as numerous as your cities, O Judah."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The idols did them no good in the time of crisis. "Among heathen nations every city had its tutelary deity. Judah, far sunk in idolatry, had adopted this custom" (Clarke). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Bible.org (Utley):** This refers either to the local Baals (cf. 11:13) or, as learned from Ugaritic literature, the Canaanite pantheon which had 250 gods. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

## Verses 29–37: God's Final Pleading and Coming Judgment

**v. 29 — "Why do you bring a case against Me? You have all rebelled against Me," declares the LORD.**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God tested the repentance of Israel to see if they would return to Him through difficulty, since earlier He had spoken of how they would turn to Him only to escape consequences, not out of true repentance. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "Plead with me" — that is, contend with Me for afflicting you (vv. 23, 35). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 30 — "I have struck your sons in vain; they accepted no discipline. Your own sword has devoured your prophets like a voracious lion."**

- **JFB:** The chastisement was futile (cf. Jer 5:3; 6:29; Isa 1:5; 9:13). "Your... sword... devoured... prophets" (2 Chr 36:16; Neh 9:26; Matt 23:29, 31). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God's people were guilty of rejecting and murdering the prophets. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

**v. 31 — "You people of this generation, consider the word of the LORD: Have I been a wilderness to Israel or a land of dense darkness? Why do My people say, 'We are free to roam; we will come to You no more'?"**

- **JFB:** "The Hebrew collocation is, 'O, the generation, ye,' that is, 'O ye who now live.' The generation needed only to be named, to call its degeneracy to view, so palpable was it." "We are lords" — better, "We ramble at large" (from a different Hebrew root), without restraint pursuing idolatrous lusts. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God's people were guilty of pride, believing they didn't need to humble themselves before God. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

**v. 32 — "Does a maiden forget her jewelry or a bride her wedding sash? Yet My people have forgotten Me for days without number."**

- **JFB:** "Oriental women greatly pride themselves on their ornaments (compare Isa 61:10)." "Attire" — girdles for the breast. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Spurgeon (sermon "Gadding About"):** Spurgeon cites this verse as one of the expressions of divine astonishment at Israel's unfaithfulness, together with vv. 10–12. The point is the sheer unnaturalness of forgetting God — as unthinkable as a bride forgetting her wedding attire. [https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/gadding-about]

**v. 33 — "How skillfully you pursue love! Even the most immoral of women could learn from your ways."**

- **JFB:** "Why trimmest" — Maurer translates "How skilfully thou dost prepare thy way," but "trimmest" best suits the image of one decking herself as a harlot. "Even the wicked harlots... even the Gentiles who are wicked, thou teachest to be still more so" (Grotius). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Guzik applies this verse directly to modern sexual immorality: "people today call sinful pursuits beautiful, teach them to others, and leave innocent lives damaged, yet claim innocence before God." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

**v. 34 — "Moreover, your skirts are stained with the blood of the innocent poor, though you did not find them breaking in. But in spite of all these things..."**

- **JFB:** "Also — not only art thou polluted with idolatry, but also with the guilt of shedding innocent blood" (Maurer). Some translate "even in thy skirts... there is no part of thee (not even thy skirts) that is not stained with innocent blood" (Jer 19:4; 2 Kgs 21:16; Ps 106:38). "I did not need to 'search deep' to find proof of thy guilt; for it was 'upon all these' thy skirts. Not in deep caverns didst thou perpetrate these atrocities, but openly in the vale of Hinnom." [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

- **Bridgeway:** "A person might happen to shed blood in defending himself against a robber, but the people of Judah attack the poor and helpless simply because they love violence." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-2.html]

**v. 35 — "...you say, 'I am innocent. Surely His anger will turn from me.' Behold, I will judge you, because you say, 'I have not sinned.'"**

- **Bible.org (Utley):** Self-deception is the real problem here. They thought they were religious and worshipping YHWH, but their claim of innocence was false. The verse picks up the same theme as v. 23. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

- **Bridgeway:** "Their consciences have become so dull that they cannot see their wrongdoing." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/jeremiah-2.html]

**v. 36 — "How unstable you are, constantly changing your ways! You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "To gad about is to bounce about on an irregular course. The New Living Translation has this, 'First here, then there — you flit from one ally to another asking for help.' There was no reason for them to gad about — they should have gone straight away to trusting the LORD." Guzik cites Spurgeon's sermon "Gadding About," in which Spurgeon focused on two ideas: (1) the word "you" — this was Israel, the wife of Yahweh; why should she do this? (2) the word "why" — God requested a reason to account for their gadding about. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **Spurgeon:** In his sermon "Gadding About," Spurgeon applies this to believers: "We are married unto Christ... Now it is to us who own this marriage union... that the Well-beloved says, 'Why gaddest thou about so much?'" He also applies it to the unconverted: "You may gad about as long as you will, but you will never gain peace, except by simple faith in Jesus." [https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/gadding-about]

- **JFB:** "Gaddest" — runnest to and fro, now seeking help from Assyria (2 Chr 28:16–21), now from Egypt (Jer 37:7–8; Isa 30:3). [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**v. 37 — "Moreover, you will leave that place with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those you trust; you will not prosper by their help."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God promised to bring their trust in Egypt to nothing; without national repentance, they would go forth as captive slaves with hands on their heads — a gesture of mourning and defeat. God would not honor their alliances with Egypt or any other foreign power. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

- **JFB:** "Him" — Egypt. "Hands upon... head" — expressive of mourning (2 Sam 13:19). "In them" — in those stays in which thou trustest. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The sources available do not reveal sharp denominational disputes over this chapter; Jeremiah 2 is broadly agreed upon across evangelical traditions. However, several distinct emphases can be noted:

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon's sermons on Jeremiah 2 (especially "Gadding About" on v. 36) emphasize personal conversion and simple faith in Christ. He reads the gadding about of Israel as a picture of the sinner trying every remedy except Christ, and of the believer looking to earthly crutches instead of the heavenly Bridegroom. His application is directly evangelistic — calling the sinner to "renounce all other hopes, and fly away to the wounds of Jesus." [https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/gadding-about]

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik reads vv. 20–25 literally — not merely as poetic metaphor but as describing "real, degrading spiritual and moral compromise." He directly applies vv. 33–37 to modern sexual immorality. The emphasis is on the experiential dimension: God "remembers" the better days and feels the pain of Israel's betrayal. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-2/]

**Reformed (JFB):** JFB stresses divine sovereignty and covenant. The "kindness" of v. 2 is interpreted as God's kindness *toward* Israel (not Israel's toward God), since Israel "from the first showed perversity." The emphasis falls on God's initiative, God's glory, and the judicial nature of the lawsuit. [https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_002.cfm]

**Evangelical/Academic (Bible.org / Utley):** Utley provides the most technical treatment — Hebrew vocabulary, text-critical notes (LXX variants, Masoretic suggestions), and ANE background. His approach is broadly evangelical but with a scholarly method that leaves room for the reader to weigh evidence. [https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-2]

**Gill (Particular Baptist, 18th century):** Gill reads the chapter Christologically: the "fountain of living waters" is Christ (Song 4:15); the "cisterns" include "moral duties, and evangelical services, when depended on; yea, acts of faith, when they are rested in, and the object not so much regarded." His concern is with works-righteousness even within the believing community. The "kindness of thy youth" he reads as applicable to the believer at first conversion, when love is "very ardent and fervent." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/2.htm]

## Summary of Key Themes Across Commentators

1. **The marriage metaphor:** Virtually all commentators note that Jeremiah draws on Hosea's imagery of God as Husband and Israel as unfaithful wife. The "devotion of your youth" recalls the honeymoon period of the Exodus and Sinai covenant.

2. **The two evils (v. 13):** This is the chapter's theological center. The sin is twofold: forsaking God (the fountain) *and* attempting self-provision (broken cisterns). Every source treats this as the classic diagnosis of idolatry and self-reliance.

3. **The unnaturalness of apostasy (vv. 10–12):** Pagan nations remain loyal to their non-existent gods; only Israel exchanges the true God for idols. This astonishes even the heavens.

4. **Self-deception (vv. 23, 35):** Despite overwhelming evidence of guilt, the people claim innocence. This theme runs through multiple commentators as a warning about the hardness of the human heart.

5. **Political alliances as spiritual adultery (vv. 14–19, 36–37):** Trust in Egypt and Assyria is not mere bad foreign policy — it is forsaking the LORD, the true fountain. The "gadding about" between alliances mirrors spiritual instability.
